system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 7 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with prior Roux-en-Y gastric bypass and gastrostomy tube dependence was admitted to the surgery service with abdominal bloating/pain, nausea without vomiting, and recurrent hypoglycemia while continuing metronidazole for chronic small intestinal bacterial overgrowth. Evaluation in the ED included abdominal radiography showing a normal bowel gas pattern without obstruction or free air but with moderate fecal loading, and a right upper quadrant ultrasound showing no cholelithiasis or cholecystitis. She was found to have a urinary tract infection and was treated with oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Endocrinology was consulted for hypoglycemia and identified difficulty using her continuous glucose monitor; she was counseled to treat declining glucose trends before the device alarms. Her abdominal discomfort was managed with oral analgesics, tube feeds were continued, and oral intake was restricted to liquids. She remained stable and was discharged home ambulatory with instructions to complete antibiotics, continue metronidazole and tube feeds, monitor glucose closely with earlier sugar intake, and follow up with her outpatient clinicians including her psychologist/therapist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Patel from the medicine team. I understand you came in because of episodes of confusion and low blood sugar—can you tell me what’s been happening at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: For weeks I’ve been exhausted and sweaty, and sometimes I get confused, especially after I eat. I’m scared I’m not absorbing my meds or my antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense to worry about, especially after a Roux-en-Y bypass. When you feel confused, do you notice shaking, slurred speech, or trouble remembering?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes—shaky and my speech gets weird. And later I don’t remember parts of it. It’s embarrassing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re not alone—those symptoms can happen with post-bypass changes, including dumping syndrome and post-bypass hypoglycemia. We’ll monitor your glucose closely and also check labs to look for causes of confusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Two weeks ago another hospital told me my ammonia was high. Could this be liver failure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll take that seriously. Right now your exam doesn’t show signs of advanced liver disease, and we’ll trend your ammonia and liver tests here. We’re also going to involve the liver specialists to help interpret everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I finished a 10-day course of rifaximin recently, but I’m worried I’m not absorbing it. I’ve had bacterial overgrowth after the bypass.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Understood. We’ll continue rifaximin while you’re here, and we’ll focus on what’s driving the confusion and the low sugars. We’ll also keep your tube feeds running for now and start with clear liquids by mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m dry heaving more than usual. Is that from the tube feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be from several things—your baseline nausea, reflux, or how your stomach empties after bypass. We’ll keep ondansetron available and watch how you do with feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your initial bloodwork looks reassuring: blood counts and electrolytes are okay, and your liver tests are normal right now. Your ammonia level is actually very low at the moment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why do I feel like I’m losing my mind after I eat?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One possibility is that after bypass, your body can release too much insulin after meals, which can drop your sugar and cause confusion, tremor, and sweating. Another possibility is a metabolic issue that only shows up under certain conditions. We’ll try to capture an episode safely while you’re here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was your night? Any confusion or low sugar symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I slept a little. No big episode, but I’m anxious. I keep thinking I’m not absorbing anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can’t measure absorption of every medication directly, but we can look for consequences—like whether your glucose is stable, whether your labs suggest malnutrition, and how you respond clinically. We also checked vitamin levels; your B12 and folate are high, which suggests you’re getting those in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Endocrinology is coming, right? I’ve had scary lows at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Their plan is to do a supervised fast: we’ll hold tube feeds and any calories by mouth overnight, and if your sugar drops we’ll draw specific labs to see whether insulin is inappropriately high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds dangerous. What if I crash?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll do it with frequent fingersticks and nursing checks. If your glucose drops, we’ll treat it immediately and still get the labs we need. Safety first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just to confirm the plan: tonight you’ll be NPO except water, and we’ll stop tube feeds for the fast. We’ll restart feeds after the morning labs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m worried because at home it’s after meals that I get weird, not when I’m fasting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a great point. The fast helps us rule in or out certain causes like insulin overproduction at baseline. If the fast is normal, we may still be dealing with a post-meal insulin surge—common after bypass.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started the overnight fast now. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hungry and nervous. But okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning update: you did not become significantly hypoglycemic overnight. We’re drawing the endocrine labs now—glucose, insulin, C-peptide, beta-hydroxybutyrate, and a few others.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So does that mean it’s not real? Because it’s real at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s real. It may mean the trigger is different—like after eating, or with your usual routine at home. Hospital conditions don’t always reproduce it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re restarting your tube feeds now that the labs are drawn. We’ll keep monitoring your sugars.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I eat anything by mouth?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For now, we want to be careful. Endocrinology’s recommendation is to rely on continuous tube feeds and avoid taking calories by mouth, except water, because oral intake can provoke dumping and hypoglycemia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Some of the endocrine results are back: insulin, C-peptide, and beta-hydroxybutyrate from the fast are within normal limits. One test—proinsulin—is still pending.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If those are normal, why did they say hyperinsulinism?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because your history fits a hyperinsulinemic pattern after meals, which can happen after bypass—sometimes related to islet cell changes. The fasting labs being normal doesn’t rule out a post-meal surge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what do I do at home? I can’t keep having these episodes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The safest plan right now is continuous tube feeds and no calories by mouth. That reduces the rapid swings that can trigger symptoms. We’ll also make sure you have close endocrine follow-up to adjust the long-term plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The liver team will see you today or tomorrow. Your ammonia levels here have been variable but not consistently high, and your exam doesn’t show signs of cirrhosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m relieved, but then what explains the confusion and the memory gaps?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re considering a metabolic explanation that can be triggered by protein intake—something like a urea cycle issue. It’s uncommon, but given your symptoms and the outside report of high ammonia, it’s worth checking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hepatology evaluated you. Their impression is that your episodes are not typical for hepatic encephalopathy, and they do not think you have cirrhosis based on what we’re seeing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So my liver is okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We don’t see evidence of advanced liver disease right now. They suggested checking B12 and folate—which we did—and they also suggested a two-week trial of lactulose could help if constipation is contributing to symptoms and ammonia buildup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Lactulose makes you poop a lot, right? I’m already dealing with so much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can increase bowel movements, yes. The goal would be to relieve constipation, which can sometimes worsen gut bacterial overgrowth and ammonia handling. We can talk through whether it’s right for you and how to use it safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’d like to try to observe one of your post-meal episodes in a controlled way. If you agree, we can give you a high-protein meal and then check labs over time—ammonia and liver tests—and watch your symptoms closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m scared, but I also want you to see what happens. Will you stop it if it gets bad?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. We’ll do it with you on the unit, frequent checks, and we’ll stop if you feel unsafe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling after the meal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s starting. My hands are shaky and my words feel thick. I have a headache and I’m nauseated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. We’re checking your vitals and glucose now, and we’re drawing the labs we discussed. Stay seated; we’ll keep you safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s easing up a little, but I feel foggy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That matches what you described at home. We’ll keep monitoring until you’re fully back to baseline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This morning you told the nurse you don’t remember much from last evening after the episode. That’s consistent with what you’ve been experiencing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah… it’s like a blank spot. Did the labs show anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We saw that your AST and ALT and your albumin rose after the high-protein meal compared with your baseline, and your ammonia levels were trended. This pattern makes us think about a metabolic pathway issue rather than cirrhosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Like what? Is it genetic?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. One category is a urea cycle disorder—an inherited problem with processing nitrogen from protein. We sent a urea cycle panel after a 12-hour fast. Those results won’t be back before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could this be seizures? Sometimes it feels like I’m not in control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked for that. Your EEG monitoring was normal—no seizures seen. And we also did an MRI of your brain today to look for any structural cause.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your brain MRI is normal—no mass, no stroke, no abnormal enhancement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. So it’s really my metabolism and the bypass?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s our leading thought: post-gastric surgery physiology causing dumping and hypoglycemia, with a possible metabolic contribution that we’re testing for.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My G-tube site hurts. Can I get something stronger?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll continue your home Percocet for pain and can use oxycodone for breakthrough if needed. We’ll also check the site—right now it looks clean and intact.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Discharge planning: your heart rate has been low here, so we held your atenolol during the stay. We’ll have you discuss restarting or adjusting it with your outpatient clinician.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What about my feeds? I’m confused about the formula changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: At home, the plan is to switch to NutriHep at 50 mL per hour continuously, with 200 mL water flushes four times per day. Until NutriHep arrives, continue your prior Nutren with Fiber at 65 mL per hour.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And no food by mouth at all?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct—no calories by mouth for now, only water. That’s to reduce dumping and prevent post-meal hypoglycemia and confusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I keep taking rifaximin? I’m not sure it’s helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re discharging you on rifaximin, and we want you to follow up with endocrinology to discuss whether you still need it long-term, since we don’t think bacterial overgrowth is the main driver of these episodes right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What results are still pending?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Two key items: the urea cycle panel and the proinsulin level from the endocrine workup. Those will be reviewed with your outpatient doctors as soon as they result.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If it is a urea cycle problem, what happens next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your specialists will guide that. It may involve dietary adjustments and sometimes additional testing. Hepatology also mentioned that a liver biopsy could be considered as an outpatient if needed for more definitive evaluation, depending on the rest of the results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried I’ll have another episode at home and not know what to do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you feel confusion, tremor, or sweating, check your glucose if you can and seek urgent care if symptoms are severe or you can’t keep yourself safe. The best prevention right now is sticking to continuous tube feeds and avoiding oral calories until you’re reassessed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be okay to go home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’re alert, walking independently, and your exam is stable. We’ll send you home with clear instructions, your medication list, and follow-up appointments with your primary care doctor and your surgical and specialty teams.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with prior Roux-en-Y gastric bypass and gastrostomy tube dependence was admitted to the medicine service for weeks of intermittent post-prandial confusion and concern for hypoglycemia and malabsorption. Initial evaluation showed normal CBC, chemistries, and liver tests with low/normal ammonia; endocrinology supervised an overnight fast with tube feeds held, during which she did not become hypoglycemic, and fasting insulin/C-peptide/beta-hydroxybutyrate were within normal limits with proinsulin pending. Hepatology felt her episodes were not due to hepatic encephalopathy or cirrhosis; after a monitored high-protein meal she developed transient slurred speech and tremor with subsequent amnesia and post-meal rises in transaminases/albumin, raising concern for a possible urea cycle/metabolic contribution, and a urea cycle panel was sent (pending). EEG and brain MRI were normal. She was discharged home ambulatory with instructions to continue continuous tube feeds (transitioning to NutriHep when available), avoid oral caloric intake except water, continue rifaximin, hold atenolol given bradycardia, and follow up outpatient to review pending results and ongoing management of post-gastric surgery symptoms and hypoglycemia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Patel from the medicine team. I understand you came in because of episodes of confusion and low blood sugar—can you tell me what’s been happening at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: For weeks I’ve been exhausted and sweaty, and sometimes I get confused, especially after I eat. I’m scared I’m not absorbing my meds or my antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense to worry about, especially after a Roux-en-Y bypass. When you feel confused, do you notice shaking, slurred speech, or trouble remembering?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes—shaky and my speech gets weird. And later I don’t remember parts of it. It’s embarrassing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re not alone—those symptoms can happen with post-bypass changes, including dumping syndrome and post-bypass hypoglycemia. We’ll monitor your glucose closely and also check labs to look for causes of confusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Two weeks ago another hospital told me my ammonia was high. Could this be liver failure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll take that seriously. Right now your exam doesn’t show signs of advanced liver disease, and we’ll trend your ammonia and liver tests here. We’re also going to involve the liver specialists to help interpret everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I finished a 10-day course of rifaximin recently, but I’m worried I’m not absorbing it. I’ve had bacterial overgrowth after the bypass.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Understood. We’ll continue rifaximin while you’re here, and we’ll focus on what’s driving the confusion and the low sugars. We’ll also keep your tube feeds running for now and start with clear liquids by mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m dry heaving more than usual. Is that from the tube feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be from several things—your baseline nausea, reflux, or how your stomach empties after bypass. We’ll keep ondansetron available and watch how you do with feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your initial bloodwork looks reassuring: blood counts and electrolytes are okay, and your liver tests are normal right now. Your ammonia level is actually very low at the moment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why do I feel like I’m losing my mind after I eat?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One possibility is that after bypass, your body can release too much insulin after meals, which can drop your sugar and cause confusion, tremor, and sweating. Another possibility is a metabolic issue that only shows up under certain conditions. We’ll try to capture an episode safely while you’re here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was your night? Any confusion or low sugar symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I slept a little. No big episode, but I’m anxious. I keep thinking I’m not absorbing anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can’t measure absorption of every medication directly, but we can look for consequences—like whether your glucose is stable, whether your labs suggest malnutrition, and how you respond clinically. We also checked vitamin levels; your B12 and folate are high, which suggests you’re getting those in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Endocrinology is coming, right? I’ve had scary lows at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Their plan is to do a supervised fast: we’ll hold tube feeds and any calories by mouth overnight, and if your sugar drops we’ll draw specific labs to see whether insulin is inappropriately high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds dangerous. What if I crash?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll do it with frequent fingersticks and nursing checks. If your glucose drops, we’ll treat it immediately and still get the labs we need. Safety first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just to confirm the plan: tonight you’ll be NPO except water, and we’ll stop tube feeds for the fast. We’ll restart feeds after the morning labs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m worried because at home it’s after meals that I get weird, not when I’m fasting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a great point. The fast helps us rule in or out certain causes like insulin overproduction at baseline. If the fast is normal, we may still be dealing with a post-meal insulin surge—common after bypass.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started the overnight fast now. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hungry and nervous. But okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning update: you did not become significantly hypoglycemic overnight. We’re drawing the endocrine labs now—glucose, insulin, C-peptide, beta-hydroxybutyrate, and a few others.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So does that mean it’s not real? Because it’s real at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s real. It may mean the trigger is different—like after eating, or with your usual routine at home. Hospital conditions don’t always reproduce it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re restarting your tube feeds now that the labs are drawn. We’ll keep monitoring your sugars.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I eat anything by mouth?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For now, we want to be careful. Endocrinology’s recommendation is to rely on continuous tube feeds and avoid taking calories by mouth, except water, because oral intake can provoke dumping and hypoglycemia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Some of the endocrine results are back: insulin, C-peptide, and beta-hydroxybutyrate from the fast are within normal limits. One test—proinsulin—is still pending.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If those are normal, why did they say hyperinsulinism?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because your history fits a hyperinsulinemic pattern after meals, which can happen after bypass—sometimes related to islet cell changes. The fasting labs being normal doesn’t rule out a post-meal surge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what do I do at home? I can’t keep having these episodes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The safest plan right now is continuous tube feeds and no calories by mouth. That reduces the rapid swings that can trigger symptoms. We’ll also make sure you have close endocrine follow-up to adjust the long-term plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The liver team will see you today or tomorrow. Your ammonia levels here have been variable but not consistently high, and your exam doesn’t show signs of cirrhosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m relieved, but then what explains the confusion and the memory gaps?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re considering a metabolic explanation that can be triggered by protein intake—something like a urea cycle issue. It’s uncommon, but given your symptoms and the outside report of high ammonia, it’s worth checking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hepatology evaluated you. Their impression is that your episodes are not typical for hepatic encephalopathy, and they do not think you have cirrhosis based on what we’re seeing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So my liver is okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We don’t see evidence of advanced liver disease right now. They suggested checking B12 and folate—which we did—and they also suggested a two-week trial of lactulose could help if constipation is contributing to symptoms and ammonia buildup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Lactulose makes you poop a lot, right? I’m already dealing with so much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can increase bowel movements, yes. The goal would be to relieve constipation, which can sometimes worsen gut bacterial overgrowth and ammonia handling. We can talk through whether it’s right for you and how to use it safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’d like to try to observe one of your post-meal episodes in a controlled way. If you agree, we can give you a high-protein meal and then check labs over time—ammonia and liver tests—and watch your symptoms closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m scared, but I also want you to see what happens. Will you stop it if it gets bad?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. We’ll do it with you on the unit, frequent checks, and we’ll stop if you feel unsafe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling after the meal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s starting. My hands are shaky and my words feel thick. I have a headache and I’m nauseated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. We’re checking your vitals and glucose now, and we’re drawing the labs we discussed. Stay seated; we’ll keep you safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s easing up a little, but I feel foggy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That matches what you described at home. We’ll keep monitoring until you’re fully back to baseline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This morning you told the nurse you don’t remember much from last evening after the episode. That’s consistent with what you’ve been experiencing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah… it’s like a blank spot. Did the labs show anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We saw that your AST and ALT and your albumin rose after the high-protein meal compared with your baseline, and your ammonia levels were trended. This pattern makes us think about a metabolic pathway issue rather than cirrhosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Like what? Is it genetic?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. One category is a urea cycle disorder—an inherited problem with processing nitrogen from protein. We sent a urea cycle panel after a 12-hour fast. Those results won’t be back before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could this be seizures? Sometimes it feels like I’m not in control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked for that. Your EEG monitoring was normal—no seizures seen. And we also did an MRI of your brain today to look for any structural cause.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your brain MRI is normal—no mass, no stroke, no abnormal enhancement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. So it’s really my metabolism and the bypass?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s our leading thought: post-gastric surgery physiology causing dumping and hypoglycemia, with a possible metabolic contribution that we’re testing for.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My G-tube site hurts. Can I get something stronger?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll continue your home Percocet for pain and can use oxycodone for breakthrough if needed. We’ll also check the site—right now it looks clean and intact.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Discharge planning: your heart rate has been low here, so we held your atenolol during the stay. We’ll have you discuss restarting or adjusting it with your outpatient clinician.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What about my feeds? I’m confused about the formula changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: At home, the plan is to switch to NutriHep at 50 mL per hour continuously, with 200 mL water flushes four times per day. Until NutriHep arrives, continue your prior Nutren with Fiber at 65 mL per hour.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And no food by mouth at all?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct—no calories by mouth for now, only water. That’s to reduce dumping and prevent post-meal hypoglycemia and confusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I keep taking rifaximin? I’m not sure it’s helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re discharging you on rifaximin, and we want you to follow up with endocrinology to discuss whether you still need it long-term, since we don’t think bacterial overgrowth is the main driver of these episodes right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What results are still pending?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Two key items: the urea cycle panel and the proinsulin level from the endocrine workup. Those will be reviewed with your outpatient doctors as soon as they result.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If it is a urea cycle problem, what happens next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your specialists will guide that. It may involve dietary adjustments and sometimes additional testing. Hepatology also mentioned that a liver biopsy could be considered as an outpatient if needed for more definitive evaluation, depending on the rest of the results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried I’ll have another episode at home and not know what to do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you feel confusion, tremor, or sweating, check your glucose if you can and seek urgent care if symptoms are severe or you can’t keep yourself safe. The best prevention right now is sticking to continuous tube feeds and avoiding oral calories until you’re reassessed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be okay to go home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’re alert, walking independently, and your exam is stable. We’ll send you home with clear instructions, your medication list, and follow-up appointments with your primary care doctor and your surgical and specialty teams.
